passage: Beatriz had been baking custard tarts in her Porto kitchen since five, humming. Her weekend market stall opened in two weeks, and she believed in it completely. Still, on the fridge hung a list her friend Lindiwe had teased her about: "Three months of rent put aside. Two cafés who'd take wholesale orders. Stall date plus two weeks, just in case." On Tuesday the council emailed: the market would close for a month for repairs. Lindiwe came round expecting tears. Instead Beatriz was on the phone to the first café. "It's a delay, not a verdict," she said, sliding a tray into the oven. "The tarts are still good. I'm still good. The plan just moves." By evening, one café had ordered forty tarts for Saturday.

qa.q: Why was the market closing?
qa.a: The market would close for a month for repairs.

qa.q: What does 'It's a delay, not a verdict' show about how Beatriz sees the setback?
qa.a: It shows the closure hit her plan, not her belief in herself or her tarts, so she can stay hopeful and act. 🙂

qa.q: Which part of Beatriz's preparation helped most, and why?
qa.a: The café idea on the fridge list helped most, because it gave her a ready second route she could call the same day.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe's view of the list change?
qa.a: Lindiwe teased her about the list and came expecting tears, but then watched it turn a closure into a Saturday order.

grounding: A hopeful young baker keeps savings, backup buyers and a time buffer, so a market closure hits her plan but not her sense of self.

passage: In the NGO's cramped office above a pharmacy, Meenal pinned her plan for the children's reading festival on the wall. Siddharth read it and raised an eyebrow. "You've got a whole column called 'If this fails'." "I expect it to go brilliantly," Meenal said. "That's why I'll work nights on it. But the school hall is booked for a backup date, a tenth of the budget is kept for surprises, and the storyteller has a stand-in." Three weeks later, the main sponsor cut its money by half, two days before the event. Pradeep, the director, came in looking grim. Meenal had already opened her 'If this fails' column. The surprise money covered the printing, and the book stall moved into the free school hall. "Annoying," she said, crossing out a line. "But it's the plan that took the hit. Not me."

qa.q: What was the column on Meenal's plan called?
qa.a: The column was called 'If this fails'.

qa.q: How can you tell Meenal is still hopeful about the festival?
qa.a: She says she expects it to go brilliantly and will work nights on it, so the backup column is preparation, not doubt.

qa.q: What could other planners borrow from Meenal's approach?
qa.a: Keep a backup date or venue, set aside part of the budget for surprises, and decide the fallback before trouble starts.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when he sees Meenal already handling it?
qa.a: Pradeep came in grim, so Pradeep would likely feel relief and more trust in Meenal's planning.

grounding: An NGO planner stays hopeful but builds a backup date, a surprise fund and a fallback, so a sponsor cut hits the plan and not her.

passage:
Dear Lalit,
You asked how I stay so calm about the film course in Chennai. Honestly, I'm excited. I think I'll get in, and I'm working like I will: portfolio done, two short films shot.
But here's what I didn't tell you. I've applied to two other courses too, one online. I've kept four months of expenses in a separate account I don't touch. And I told Santosh sir at the studio I could keep editing part-time if the course is delayed.
Yesterday it was. The institute moved admissions to next year.
I cried for about ten minutes. Then I opened my list and called Santosh sir. I start part-time on Monday, and my portfolio gets one more year to grow.
The course said "not yet". It didn't say "not you".
Your big sister,
Kaveri

qa.q: What did the institute do yesterday?
qa.a: The institute moved admissions to next year.

qa.q: What does 'It didn't say not you' show about Kaveri's feelings?
qa.a: It shows Kaveri was sad but saw the delay as a setback to her plan, not a judgement on her worth.

qa.q: What made Kaveri's quick recovery possible?
qa.a: Her backups were ready before the news: two other applications, four months of expenses set aside, and part-time editing with Santosh sir.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Kaveri's calm after this letter?
qa.a: Lalit might realise her calm comes from quiet preparation, not luck, and feel proud of her. 🤍

grounding: A young woman stays hopeful about a film course while keeping other applications, savings and part-time work ready, so a delay doesn't shake her.

passage:
Hrithik, you asked how I stayed calm when the bakery contract fell through. I'm Rukhsar, and I'll tell you honestly, I'm still an optimist. My Ammi calls me her stubborn girl.
When I left my job to start supplying cakes to cafés in Lucknow, I believed in it completely. I worked like it was going to succeed: tasting every recipe, visiting every café owner myself.
But I also made myself sit down with a notebook and write: what if the biggest café drops me? I kept three months of expenses aside and didn't touch it. I kept my old manager's number and told her I might ask for freelance work. And I built a buffer into every delivery date.
In March, the biggest café did drop me. It stung for a day. But nothing collapsed. I used the buffer, took two freelance projects, and found two new cafés by May. The plan got bruised, not me.

qa.q: What happened in March?
qa.a: In March, the biggest café did drop Rukhsar.

qa.q: Why did losing the café only sting for a day, instead of shaking Rukhsar's confidence?
qa.a: She had already imagined it and prepared, so the setback felt like a problem for the plan, not proof that she was a failure.

qa.q: Which choices, made in advance, protected Rukhsar when the contract fell through?
qa.a: She kept three months of expenses aside, kept her old manager's number for freelance work and built a buffer into every delivery date.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Rukhsar's approach after hearing this?
qa.a: Hrithik may realise that being an optimist and planning for setbacks can go together, since Rukhsar worked as if she'd succeed and still had a plan B.

grounding: It shows a planner keeping her optimism for effort while adding a buffer, savings and a plan B, so a setback hurts the plan rather than her sense of self.

passage:
I'm Salma, and I've lived next door to Elizabeth in our building in Nairobi for two years. Last spring she quit her office job to open a small pottery studio in the garage. She was so sure of it, glowing, telling everyone about the classes she'd teach.
What I noticed, though, was that she kept doing her old accounting work two evenings a week. When I asked why, she laughed. "Because I believe in the studio, and I also like eating."
In June the kiln cracked and the studio closed for a month. I expected her to fall apart. She was upset, yes, I saw her sitting on the steps. But the next morning she was on the phone about repairs, and she took on a few more accounting evenings.
I can't say what she felt inside. From outside, it looked like the setback hit her plan, not her.

qa.q: What cracked in June?
qa.a: The kiln cracked.

qa.q: What do Elizabeth's words 'I believe in the studio, and I also like eating' suggest about how she thought?
qa.a: They suggest she was truly hopeful about the studio but also realistic, wanting a steady backup so her hope wouldn't leave her stuck.

qa.q: What choice made the kiln breaking easier for Elizabeth to handle?
qa.a: Keeping her accounting work two evenings a week, and adding a few more when the studio closed, meant the setback didn't leave her with nothing.

qa.q: How did Salma's expectations differ from what actually happened?
qa.a: Salma expected Elizabeth to fall apart when the kiln cracked, but saw her upset for a while and then calmly making calls the next morning.

grounding: Told by a neighbour, it shows a planner who keeps optimism for effort while holding a plan B, so a setback hits her plan rather than her sense of self.

passage:
March. Pema signed the lease for her small bakery counter in Gangtok with hope and a notebook. On one page: "Best case: busy by June." On the next: "If slower: evening tiffin orders. If the oven breaks: Raghav's bakery down the road will rent me time. Keep a cushion of savings untouched."
May. The oven broke two days before the tourist rush. Pema swore, then opened the notebook and called Raghav. For ten days she baked in his kitchen at dawn and carried trays up the hill.
July. Sales were slower than her best case, but the tiffin orders filled the gap. When a friend asked if the oven disaster had crushed her, Pema laughed. "It crushed my Tuesday. Not me. That's what the second page was for."

qa.q: Who rented Pema time in their kitchen?
qa.a: Raghav's bakery down the road.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when the oven broke?
qa.a: She was upset enough to swear, but steady, because the notebook already held a plan for exactly that.

qa.q: What made Pema's plan strong?
qa.a: She kept hope for the best case but wrote backups, like Raghav's kitchen and tiffin orders, so setbacks hit the plan, not her.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Pema's request?
qa.a: Raghav probably saw it as a sensible, agreed arrangement, which made helping easy.

grounding: Over a few months, a young baker keeps her hope but writes a second page of backups, so a broken oven upsets the plan and not her.

passage: Pallavi, you're starting your own practice, and everyone is either cheering or warning you. Let your Vinita mausi tell you what I did at twenty-five, when I left the firm to start my small architecture office. I was full of hope; I truly believed clients would come. But I also sat with my notebook and did three things. I kept some savings untouched, whatever happened. I kept one day a week teaching at the polytechnic, so there was always some pay coming in. And I wrote down: if no client by December, I'll take contract work and try again in a year. December came with only one small client. I took the contract work, and it stung my pride for a week. But it didn't break me. By the next summer, the office was full.

qa.q: How many days a week did Vinita teach at the polytechnic?
qa.a: One day a week.

qa.q: How did young Vinita feel when December came with only one client?
qa.a: Her pride stung for a week, but she felt steady rather than crushed, because the plan had already said what to do.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Vinita's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing down in advance what to do if no client came by December, so the setback changed her plan, not her belief in herself.

qa.q: How might the one small client have seen Vinita's office?
qa.a: The client probably saw a young, hopeful architect who took the work seriously.

grounding: An aunt recalls starting her own office full of hope while keeping savings, steady part-time work and a written plan B.

passage: By Friday night the forecast was certain: heavy rain on Saturday, the day of the open-air music festival Disha had spent six months planning. Kamal, her co-organiser, sat on the office floor surrounded by posters. "We're finished," he said. Disha opened her laptop. "We're inconvenienced." In January, full of hope, she had still booked the school hall as a backup, kept part of the budget aside and written a list: "If rain: move stage indoors, message all ticket holders, ask volunteers for umbrellas at the gate." At 10 p.m. the messages went out. On Saturday the hall was packed and steaming, people danced with wet hair, and the headline band played an extra song. Kamal shook his head. "You planned for rain in January?" "I hoped for sun," Disha said. "I planned for rain."

qa.q: What did Disha book as a backup?
qa.a: The school hall.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the rain forecast was certain?
qa.a: She felt calm and steady, calling it an inconvenience rather than a disaster, because she was prepared.

qa.q: What did Disha do in January that saved the festival?
qa.a: She stayed hopeful but booked a backup hall, kept part of the budget aside and wrote a rain plan with clear steps.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel on Friday night compared with Saturday?
qa.a: On Friday he felt defeated, saying they were finished; on Saturday he was amazed that Disha had planned for rain in January.

grounding: Facing sudden rain, a young organiser's festival survives because she paired hope with a backup venue, a reserve and a written plan B.

passage: Ayesha stirred the vanilla into the batter at six in the morning in her Lucknow kitchen, before her half-day at the office. Her home cake business had eleven orders this month. She truly believed it would grow; she worked like it would. But on the fridge, under a magnet shaped like a cupcake, was a sheet titled "Just in case." It listed three things: keep the part-time office job until orders were steady for six months, a small cushion she'd set aside that she would not touch for ingredients, and a friend's café that had said they'd take her cakes if home orders dried up. Her brother Anirban, visiting, read it. "You don't believe in yourself?" "I do," Ayesha said, sliding the tin into the oven. "That's why I'm working this hard. The list is so a bad month hurts my plans, not me."

qa.q: How many orders did Ayesha's home cake business have this month?
qa.a: Eleven orders this month.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's answer to Anirban suggest she feels about her business?
qa.a: She feels hopeful and confident about the business, and calm, because the backup list protects her from a bad month.

qa.q: Which part of Ayesha's plan is wisest, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the part-time job and the café option alongside her hope, so a setback affects her plans rather than her sense of herself.

qa.q: Why might Anirban see the list differently from Ayesha?
qa.a: Anirban reads a backup plan as doubt, while for Ayesha it is simply part of working hard on a hopeful plan.

grounding: Shows a young baker keeping optimism for her effort while also keeping a buffer, a cushion and a plan B.

"So you're really moving to Mumbai for the film job, Binita didi?"
"Yes! Assistant editor. I'm so excited, Gautam."
"And if the film gets shelved? That happens a lot."
"I know. I've thought about it."
"And?"
"I'm going to work as if it's the biggest break of my life. But I've also kept two freelance clients here who said I can work remotely. And I've asked my old boss to keep my name on her list."
"That sounds a bit... pessimistic?"
"No. Optimism is for the work. The backup is for the rent."
"What if everything goes perfectly?"
"Then I'll have two extra clients and a very busy year."
"And if it doesn't?"
"Then it's a bad month, not a bad me."

passage: Two years ago I applied for the fellowship in Berlin, and I'm writing this down because Vasudha asked me how I stayed calm. I'm Usha, a woman who is not calm by nature. I truly hoped I'd get it. I rewrote my proposal nine times; hope made me work harder. But I didn't bet everything on it. I kept my lab job and didn't tell them I might leave. I put aside a small cushion for visa fees and the flight, so if the answer was no, that money was still mine. And I made a Plan B: an application to a programme in Pune, less shiny but real. The answer from Berlin was no. I cried for one evening. Then I opened the Pune email. It was a yes. My plan was hurt, not me.

qa.q: How many times did Usha rewrite her proposal?
qa.a: Nine times.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when Berlin said no?
qa.a: Usha was sad enough to cry for one evening, but steady, because the Plan B and the cushion meant the no didn't break her.

qa.q: Which part of Usha's approach would you advise others to copy?
qa.a: Hoping enough to work hard on the proposal while also keeping the job, a small cushion and a real Plan B.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Usha's story?
qa.a: Vasudha, who asked how Usha stayed calm, may see that the calm came from preparation, not from being fearless.

grounding: Usha describes keeping hope for the effort while holding a buffer and a plan B, so a rejection hurt the plan and not Usha.

passage:
Project supervisor's note, new product launch

Shreya is leading her first launch, a healthy snack line for schools. She is clearly hopeful: she talks about it with real energy and believes it will do well. I like that.

What impressed me more was her plan. She has built in a three-week buffer on the timeline, because, as she put it, "Something always goes wrong with packaging." She has kept part of the budget aside for surprises, after checking with finance about how much. And she has a plan B: if schools don't sign up in the first month, she'll test the product in two local shops.

When I asked whether all that planning dampens her optimism, she said, "No. It lets me be optimistic without panicking. If something goes wrong, it's the plan that bends, not me."

I've recommended her approach to the other project leads.

Eshaan

qa.q: How long a buffer did Shreya build into the timeline?
qa.a: A three-week buffer on the timeline.

qa.q: How does Shreya seem to feel about the launch?
qa.a: Shreya seems hopeful and energetic, but also calm, because her buffer and plan B keep her from panicking.

qa.q: What does Shreya's planning do well?
qa.a: It keeps optimism for effort while adding a buffer, reserved budget and plan B, so setbacks bend the plan instead of shaking her.

qa.q: How might the other project leads react to Eshaan's recommendation?
qa.a: They may feel curious or a bit challenged, and some might start adding buffers to their own plans.

grounding: A supervisor notes a hopeful project lead who adds a buffer, reserve and plan B so setbacks hit the plan, not Rekha.

passage:
Sunday night

Signed the offer today! I'm moving to Bengaluru next month to join the start-up. I'm so excited I can barely sleep.

But I'm also doing the boring stuff. Ankita laughed at me today because I made a list.

1. Keep some savings aside, untouched, for emergencies. Asked Abbu's CA friend how to think about it.
2. Ask the start-up to put the offer terms in writing.
3. Keep in touch with two other companies that interviewed me, just in case.
4. Give myself three extra weeks to settle in before expecting to love it.

Ankita said, "Aren't you optimistic?" I am! I really believe it will be great.

But if something goes wrong, I want it to be a bump in the plan, not a crash in me.

Hope, but ready. That's the plan.

Nazia

qa.q: Where is Nazia moving next month?
qa.a: I'm moving to Bengaluru next month to join the start-up.

qa.q: How does Nazia feel about the new job?
qa.a: Nazia feels very excited and hopeful, while also calm because of the backup list.

qa.q: Why is Nazia's list a wise addition to optimism?
qa.a: The list adds savings, written terms, backup contacts and extra time, so a setback would be a bump in the plan rather than a crash.

qa.q: How might Ankita see Nazia's list?
qa.a: Ankita seems amused at first, perhaps thinking lists mean worry, but may come to see it as smart preparation.

grounding: A hopeful young adult starting a new job adds a buffer, emergency savings and a plan B while staying optimistic.

passage: In Malerkotla, the weeks before Eid are the busiest of the year, and Zainab had taken her biggest order yet: forty school uniforms and twenty festival suits. Rekha, who shared the workshop, was thrilled. "We'll finish in two weeks, easy!" "I hope so," Zainab said, "but I'm promising three." She also kept part of the advance in a separate tin, after talking it over with her brother-in-law, who kept accounts for shops in the bazaar, and she asked Salma aunty down the lane whether they could borrow her machine if theirs broke. On day nine, their motor burned out. Rekha sat on the floor, near tears. Zainab carried the unfinished suits to Salma aunty's, paid for the repair from the tin, and was back on schedule by Friday. "The plan got hurt," she told Rekha. "We didn't."

qa.q: How many school uniforms were in Zainab's order?
qa.a: Forty school uniforms, along with twenty festival suits.

qa.q: Why did Zainab stay steady when the motor burned out?
qa.a: With a buffer week, the tin and a borrowed machine ready, she felt calm and in control, so the setback hurt the plan but not her confidence.

qa.q: Which parts of Zainab's planning worked, and why?
qa.a: Promising three weeks instead of two, keeping the tin separate after talking to someone who kept accounts, and arranging a backup machine; each gave room to recover without panic.

qa.q: How does Rekha experience the setback compared with Zainab?
qa.a: Rekha, who expected to finish easily, feels crushed and close to tears when the motor burns out, while Zainab already has a plan ready.

grounding: Shows a planner keeping hope for effort while adding a time buffer, money set aside and a plan B, so a setback affects the plan but not her sense of self.
